However, with heavy usage on wifi or cellular broadband use it will last approximately 12-15 hrs of nonstop use- which is outstanding for me. As I write this review I've been downloading a large file, uploading my pictures to the cloud, taking and making calls, using messenger and the phone message app, as well as running a malware and virus scan in the background simultaneously. Compact budget phone. I bought the refurbished Pixel 4a back around December 2020. It was about $35 less than brand new price. It was probably only cosmetic damages and nothing to affect the performance, but being the OCD I am, I decided to return it and get a brand new one from a carrier since they were doing a $100 off promo. I've had the phone for about 8 months now and it's been a great phone, I have no problems. However, if I was going to get nit-picky, I'd say the phone has 1-2 second delays/hiccups occasionally.

However, if I was going to get nit-picky, I'd say the phone has 1-2 second delays/hiccups occasionally. I've learned to live with it, this is not a top of the line phone. Decent for the price but there are annoying tradeoffs. For the price this is really a lot of phone (nice display, good camera, 128 gig storage, 3yrs of OS upgrades). But there are several negatives you should be aware of: Battery life - OK, but not great Processor - OK, but not great Display - looks great but there is an area about 10 - 20 pixels big all around the right edge and bottom where the phone does not register any touches. Very annoying in games and any app with buttons way at the right/bottom. The Pixel Launcher takes a huge chunk of the display for Google to use as they please (can be fixed by switching to the Nova Launched, but it's annoying to have to do that) Not water proof No wireless charging I really like the smaller size and can live with the problems for a couple years, but I'll be upgrading in 3yrs...

I bought the 4 GB ram model.. I love my Moto G Plus. I bought the 4 GB ram and 64 GB storage model which makes a big difference. I would not have bought the lesser model. I have all the Amazon apps that I want, and Google apps are not hogging my phone now.

Lots of calls, Facebook, email, you tube, various productivity apps... etc. I can go pretty much 3 days between charges and when it needs it, the phone charges fast. My old Lumia needed to be charged frequently even when it was new and every night the iPhone and the Samsung Galaxy in my house are on their chargers or they are both bricks the next day. Not the Moto G Plus, but excellent batter life comes with some big tradeoffs. Processor speed. This is a harder one for me to evaluate since I was upgrading from a phone that was a couple generations old and running an antiquated OS, but this phone seems fast. I surf along with others in the family using higher end phones and don't seem to be noticeably behind and the performance well outpaces what I upgraded from. Size and dimensions.

Size and dimensions. The Moto G5 Plus has a nice balance of size and shape. It has a large screen but is not too large to hold in your hand. Wi-Fi connectivity. The Moto G5 Plus does a good job connecting and staying connected to the Wi-Fi networks at my home and office. I also can easily set it up as a hotspot and my devices connect to it via Wi-Fi and it provides a strong, wide reaching signal. Fingerprint Sensor. I had low expectations for this at the start, but the fingerprint sensor works well and is not too touchy. All it takes is basically the same pressing motion you would have to turn on an iPhone, but with the added security of the fingerprint sensor built in. Cons: It really is not a particularly good phone.

Past it's Prime. During a recent security update, my 8 month old Pixel 4a ($275) died. It could not see the sim card anymore. After 4 grueling hours in Google's warranty claim labyrinth, I finally had an appointment with you-break-we-no-fix. The guy at the counter says, I have a hairline crack that voids the warranty. Of course that is not true as the warranty specifically states: "If, in addition to a defect covered by this Limited Warranty, your Google Product also has damage which is not covered (for example, damage caused by normal wear and tear or misuse by you) then Google is only responsible for addressing the defect covered by this Limited Warranty". The good news is that I now have a decent pixel 4a webcam and a brand new Galaxy A53 5G ($349). The difference in these two phones is astounding.

The difference in these two phones is astounding. Just the Dolby Atmos sound alone is worth the A53 price of admission. The pixel phone quality was iffy at best. I used to get lots of sound breaks during my calls. It could be the difference between LTE and 5G, but the A53 is noticeably clearer and no drop outs so far. my 5G download speed is 300 Mb/s versus 45 Mb/s on pixel. Upload is 50 Mb/s versus 5 Mb/s. Camera on A53 is 64 MP versus 12 MP for pixel. Battery is 5000 mAh versus 3140 for Pixel 4a. You get the idea. The Pixel 4a is past it's Prime and for $489 on May 15, 2022, way overpriced.

Fast, but fragile and runs hot. Bought this just a few months ago. Out of the box it was great - fast and smooth, and quite like and compact. I really like phones that can be operated one-handed, and don't sit in your pocket like a brick. But there are compromises, a couple of which I knew going in. Light means a small battery, but I wasn't prepared for how quickly this phone burns power. Literally burns - the phone runs hot, even while web surfing, and heat means power consumption. Was not looking forward to the heat degradation on the battery over the next couple years. I am a heavy user (including lots of hotspot) but I came from a string of Moto G models with similar batteries, and wasn't having to do a mid-afternoon recharge with those. One more luxury you get with Moto phones is splash resistance, which this doesn't have.

The Essential Phone is an excellent phone with a few compromises. The Essential Phone is an excellent phone with a few compromises. Many tech reviews have not really done this phone justice. Let me explain why. Although the phone hardware is well designed, Essential did not include some ideal features like water-resistence, a headphone jack, and an OLED display. The truth is that these decisions were likely made to keep costs down and avoid supply hiccups. Although choosing an excellent IPS instead of an OLED display, may not seem ideal, when considering the Pixel 2 phone's OLED screen blue haze issue, and Apple's supply issue with their OLED displays, Essential made the obvious choice. During the initial rollout Essential had some hiccups in their quality control, but their real blunder was that they initially rushed the software without indicating that the phone was a "work-in-progress". This made the original price tag seem obscene and the phone unrefined.

This made the original price tag seem obscene and the phone unrefined. In addition, the camera software was a huge letdown. With the recent price adjustment and the frequent software updates, the PH-1 has become a smartphone package that is easily one of the best phone values today. It is now competitive with the Oneplus 5/5T rather than paling in comparison to the Pixel and iPhone, which are significantly more expensive. That said some folks seem to feel that the Oneplus 5T edges out the Essential PH-1 in a close race. One key thing to consider is Android Oreo. Although both phones will get Android 8, only the PH-1 will support Google's Project Treble which will allow for faster Android updates longer into the future. This means that the Oneplus may become unsupported and not get updates in the near future.

This means that the Oneplus may become unsupported and not get updates in the near future. The Essential PH-1 looks beautiful, feels well made and gets great reception. Although not number one in the camera, it takes pretty good photos. Unless you have unreasonable expectations, for the price this phone is a great deal. In my book, it is the best phone value going in 2017.

Big leap forward for me. I moved from Galaxy S7 edge to a Galaxy 10e, so I'm not sure how valuable my review would be to someone. The S10e is great. Here's a brief punch list of my impressions: Thumbprint reader on the upper right side: Some people say it is not convenient, but I think it is immeasurably better than the front lower reader on the S7 edge. On the S7 edge I have to shift my pinky to hook the bottom edge of the phone so I can re-position my hand and place thumb on the reader, then I have to move back to my normal holding position. On the S10e, my thumb is already in position- no shifting necessary. The S10e reader is much faster and accurate. Face recognition: My S7 edge did not have this feature. I had no idea how convenient face recognition could be! What a time saver!

Camera: I have only taken a few snapshots with the S10e, so I don't have anything to say. The specs of the S10e camera are better than the specs on the S7 edge camera, so I'm sure all will be fine. Summary: I bought the S10e as a "renewed" item on Amazon, and I am very happy with the phone and the price. After always being 2 to 3 generations behind in phone technology, I finally "caught-up" to the present, and did so at a reasonable price.

Samsung Galaxy S20 FE – 18 Months Later. The S20FE, redefined what it meant to be a budget flagship, and a premium mid-range device. Still, nearly 2 years later the value is still ever present. The device has been my daily driver since October of 2020, and this is my take on the handset. Keep in mind, this device launched at $700, I only paid 450$ with device trade in. Let’s go over the basic specs: - Snapdragon 865 CPU - 6GB RAM/128GB ROM or 8GB RAM/256GB ROM - Wifi 6 - 5G - 6.5 inch AMOLED display - Under-Display fingerprint sensor - 4500 MAH battery - Gorilla Glass 3 on the front display. Pros: - All-Day battery life. As the strange advertisements suggested this device can get me through a day of moderate to heavy usage. My usage time is upwards of 8 hours on some days.

Google is the next closest competitor to this standard. - Rear Camera. The back 3 cameras have been everyday champions at capturing the moments that I want to share with my friends and family. The newest iPhone’s will certainly beat this device especially in night photography, but overall its pictures are sharp, colorful (maybe a bit saturated), and high quality. Video too has been great and the camera app has useful tools to make pictures and videos even more special. Cons: - Gorilla Glass 3. Being a daily driver, this device has been everywhere with me. My last device, the galaxy s8 had Gorilla Glass 5. I am not super clumsy, but I have been known to drop my phone occasionally.

You can register a face, but it isn’t reliable in any sense and it just doesn’t hold the bar. My device had this issue at first but then a software update and calibration did fix my issue of touch sensitivity. I haven’t had any issues since. But on release, it was a bit rough. I think though, the software update fixed this issue for most individuals - Under-Display Fingerprint Sensor: This device comes with an optical fingerprint sensor under the display which is kind of futuristic. But it can be hit or miss. For me, after a few software updates it is almost always pretty solid and consistent.

For me, after a few software updates it is almost always pretty solid and consistent. There are times when my finger is on the display at a weird angle, and it won’t unlock but it is fast and mostly reliable. It is not as fast as rear-mounted scanners like on the Galaxy S8 and S9 series. But it has gotten better since release. Now, it should be a pretty okay experience to use. Overall, this device has been an amazing value for me over these past 18 months. It has gotten 2 software updates so far, and they still have 2 more to receive. The device should get up to android 14 according to Samsung’s 4 years of support. So, it still has lots of life left in it, and anyone considering this in 2022 should still buy this device.

Amazon Renewed XR with 90% battery health is actually 50% through its useful lifespan.... Got my Amazon Renewed iPhone XR from TRADEMORE. As advertised, the "renewed" phone //could// come with a 90% battery health. Yep, it showed up with a 92% battery health. If you think that's an "A" and it must have 92 more percents to go before it's dead, you're mistaken... At 80% battery health, Apple flags your phone as "significantly degraded" and notes that it is in need of service to function correctly and reliably. Around that time, Apple throttles your device performance to keep it alive on a charge. What this means is that 80% means your phone is in "hospice care" and less, you're dead. That means that a 90% battery health stat means your phone has only 50% of its remaining potential charges left before Apple deems your phone ready to leave this world.

4. CAMERA: The S5 sports a 16MP camera rear camera up from 13MP in the S4. The front facing camera remains pretty much the same at 2.1MP. The S5's 1/2.6" sensor is larger being closer in size to sensors from P&S cameras than smartphones. The AF is also speedier with the S5 due to its hybrid use of phase detection and contrast detection AF. The S5 is the first camera on a smartphone to use phase detection AF, which is commonly found in DSLR cameras. Other smartphones only use contrast detection AF that simply focuses by measuring the contrast between nearby pixels. This type of AF tends to be slower and not work well if shooting in situations where there isn't much contrast. Phase detection AF however focuses by comparing the actual light received by sensors.

Fast, beautiful, and feels great in the hand, but its camera and haptics do not do it justice. The Essential Phone is Andy Rubin's (the creator of Android) vision of what a flagship Android phone should be. The Company's marketing shows great pride in their industrial design: the premium materials (titanium, ceramic, Gorilla glass), the industrial design (minimal bezels, at least at the top and sides), the dual cameras (color and monochrome), and the accessory port (for a 360-degree camera only, for now) all take prominent place in their marketing. Essential, the company, has ambitions beyond the phone, as well. They are marketing an upcoming Essential Home product, an internet-of-things hub, as well. The Essential Phone is the Company's first product. It is a flagship phone at a premium price.

I am hopeful that Essential will improve its Camera app over time, mostly to improve its speed. For now, if you are looking for a camera that also happens to be a smartphone, this may not be the phone for you. While the screen is really cool, most apps don't know to move the status bar to the top of the phone, where the camera notch is, so the screen tends to just have a black band at the top, mirroring the actual black bezel on the bottom of the phone. Haptic feedback is weak and sounds like a tinny speaker. This is an area that the iPhone 7 absolutely blows away this phone. The iPhone's Taptic Engine makes controls feel physical, and can pinpoint exactly where your fingers are on the screen to make a tap. The mono speaker at the bottom of the phone is weak and tinny.

So I comparison shopped some mid-range Android phones (the cheap Android phones are almost worthless - one person I know had one and he couldn't apply Android updates without first deleting apps, and then re-installing them after upgrading... who wants that experience... ), and the Moto G5+ got excellent reviews. I did spring for the 64Gb model instead of the 32Gb model, as I wanted the extra storage. PROs: for the money, this is a great phone. It has a decent (not outstanding but quite decent) camera, call quality seems pretty good, battery life is decent (I'm not a power user but can get up to 3 days if I power off the phone overnight), and the turbo charge ability is great, lots of app availability.

CONs: it is, despite its features, still an Android phone - which means occasionally I will hit or do something without any idea of what exactly I did and I'll have to search the internet to find how to undo it; while there are lots of apps and most are free, many of them are very ad-laden (really, an ad after EVERY play in Words with Friends?), who knows if I'll ever have the option of installing the next version of Android; sound is rather thin (admittedly, just about every phone I've heard playing music suffers from this but my Windows phone struck me as having somewhat better sound).

Absolutely beautiful phone for the price. Initial review: Allow me to start from my user perspective: Moderate power user who also writes software, generally in an urban/suburban area. I use a Windows laptop, not a Mac. Given this perspective, I have all but never been an iPhone user. For the most part, I've been an Android user (Motorola (Atrix 4g: Froyo/GrahamCracker) & HTC (One X+: Ice Cream Sandwich/Jelly Bean)) with a period as a Windows Phone user (Nokia with Win10 Mobile). With most of these phones, I held onto them long past their prime - largely due to their build quality/capabilities. Despite some of the reviews I have read about the Essential PH-1, I was willing to try it based on their design mindset and the build quality/software layout that comes from that. Additionally, I have a negative perspective on "renting" a phone from my provider (AT&T,) so I tend to purchase my phone outright.

Additionally, I have a negative perspective on "renting" a phone from my provider (AT&T,) so I tend to purchase my phone outright. The recent price reduction (~$330) on the Essential PH-1 made it properly appealing, though I could still kick myself for missing out when it was priced at $250 during Prime Day. Suffice it to say that I will update this review as I learn its pros, its cons, and where the compromises are. [Update]: I have been able to provide some selective updates in the categories below, as I have had this now almost a week. I expect to have more updates in the near future, when\where warranted. Initial Unboxing: It is one of the nicer unboxing experiences I've had with a phone, though I am poorly equipped to compare it to the current competition.

I went over 24-hours without charging at one point and wound up with 45%. It would have long been dead if it had been my Nokia. This was after the latest OS update (again, see below), so this might have been a factor in the longevity. Performance: I have absolutely no complaints here so far. There's no bloatware and the Oreo update took about an hour, overall (including the download.) I know there were several complaints about OS behavior, et al, pertaining to what was initially released on the phone. As I waited until all the updates were done before doing anything on the phone, I probably saved myself from a number of disappointments. At this point, the phone is fast and responsive, both within applications and switching between multiple applications. More evaluation will be required here but I'm satisfied so far.

More evaluation will be required here but I'm satisfied so far. Of course, this is after coming from my Nokia, which was often painfully slow with Win10 Mobile. [General Update]: When I first got the phone, I immediately applied all relevant updates, including the OS update to Oreo 8.1. This went really well, no issues. On Day Two of having the phone, the Essential team released v9.0 (Pie) and I got the notification to update within hours of Essential posting the news on their blog. This also went very smoothly and I later found out that Essential was the first phone to get the update, even beating out the Google Pixel. That was impressive, as any other vendor will probably spend the next 3-4 months retooling the update before release. Some might view this negatively but I believe it is worthy of some kudos.

Some might view this negatively but I believe it is worthy of some kudos. One of the updates in the new version is an improved adaptive battery manager and that alone seems to be doing fairly well. Overall: As I have mentioned repeatedly here, these are my initial thoughts and observations of the PH-1. While I have a certain amount of optimism about this product, I don't believe I am going at this evaluation doe-eyed. So far, I am reasonable pleased and relieved. I've read the horror story reviews about cracked faces at the bezel, constantly dropped calls/network connectivity, poorly charging blocks, etc., so I'm happy that I am not seeing any of this initially. I am also painfully aware that I need to ferret out any specific issues quickly while I am inside the two month return window.

The face picks up smudges but no more than any other touchscreen out there. Display: Again, not having used an (AM)OLED screen before, I don't know what I am missing from the Essential's display. I'll have to get it into more scenarios where brightness is a factor. My Nokia was horrible in full daylight, so I know what "bad" can be but, in regards to my HTC One X+, I also know what "decent" can be. Sound: Again, I am aware of what "bad" can be in this category (Atrix 4g / Nokia 9500 series) but I've seen "decent" (again, the HTC One X+). Given the hardware, I think I can expect relatively close to "decent". But this being said, on a wired headset (Bose) with the headset adapter, the volume was very good. Call quality without the headset is also good.

Battery life is solid, but not the best in the market right now. You'll still be able to get a couple of days out of the S20 FE on 120Hz. Also, you can't beat the customizability of Android. With the option to install launchers/widgets plus a wealth of storage (and SD card support), you get a lot of choice with the S20 FE. The size, while much larger than I was used to, still fits in the hand really well. I would recommend getting a case and screen protector for this one though, as I have seen people shatter the screen with a single drop. But, if you've been reading up on the S20 FE at all, then you know that there are problems. First off, the virtual proximity sensor on the phone is spotty at best.

And yes, my phone (ordered in early November) has the issue too. Pretty horrendous ghosting when testing it in the touchscreen test app. There's undeniably a hardware issue with the S20 FE. There have been updates since the phone released, but none have fixed it entirely; merely a band-aid on a bloody gash. The real question is: does it affect everyday use? Will you notice it every moment you use the S20 FE? The answer to both is no, at least for me. While I'm sure it does affect certain tasks (most notably those that involve fast touches or 3+ fingers), I really haven't noticed it in actual use. Pinching/zooming with your fingers close together will cause the screen to jitter, but that's about all I've seen. If that worries you enough to pass on the S20 FE, I don't blame you.

If that worries you enough to pass on the S20 FE, I don't blame you. It really is a shame that I can't give the S20 FE a perfect 5 stars, because it does deserve it in some aspects. But with these hardware issues, there's always the worry that time will make them worse. It's a genuine worry, I get that. But even with the problems, the Samsung Galaxy S20 FE is a pretty great phone. It really does feel like a flagship phone, but with a massive price cut and a few downgrades. Only time will tell if the problems the phone has will get worse, but for right now, I'm more than happy with it. Edit (8/18/2021 sad I've dropped my rating from 4 stars to 3 stars.

6 Months Later - Finally worth another look. OVERVIEW I’ve owned more phone that I can count over the years. Since the first Android phones 8+ years ago, to the occasional iPhone, and to my now present daily driver, the Galaxy S8+. I’ll be taking that technical experience to see how the new Essential Phone (PH-1) fares in the competitive smartphone environment. It’s now been about 6 months since the PH-1 was released. It has since had a $200 price drop and countless software updates to fix some critical bugs and issues with stability, usability, and the camera. Let’s jump in!

PERFORMANCE & STABILITY Given the aforementioned stock experience, I found performance to be excellent. While forums are littered with reports of glitches, crashes, and other issues, I’ve found no such issues. Once again, it’s worth highlighting that Essential has released countless updates in effort to get to this point; which it should have been at launch. I’ve had no force closes, no stuttering, no unusual input lag, wobble, etc. If you look close enough, you can find a problem with any phone. Watching very closely, I can see the screen doesn’t respond 100% in sync with my input. However, when compared side-by-side with my Galaxy S8 Plus, it’s virtually identical in terms of responsiveness when scrolling. Except that in daily usage, it’s very clear stock android is still noticeably smoother than TouchWiz. I don’t have a Google phone handy, but from previous experience, it’s certainly on-par.

I don’t have a Google phone handy, but from previous experience, it’s certainly on-par. Once again, look closely, you’ll find a problem with every phone. Playing games or any demanding multi-tasking is handled with ease. Thanks in large part to the Snapdragon 835, 4GB of RAM, and 128GB of fast storage. No stuttering or lag; games are able to run at full speed and resolution. DISPLAY We don’t need to spend a lot of time on the display. It’s a pretty solid QHD 5.7” LCD display. There is no light bleed. While obviously not an OLED panel, contrast ratio is excellent for LCD. Viewing angles are good. The screen will noticeably dim when viewed off center, but there is no noticeable color shift. Thanks to a high resolution, images look great. Lots of detail, realistic color reproduction, etc. The LCD leans well into the cooler color temperature.

Which is to say, it’s actually usable now. Even though there are very little adjustments and features, it works. I’ve been taking lots of pictures comparing this phone to our other phones, as well as a few with the sideloaded Google Camera. As usual, the results vary wildly depending on the exact shooting conditions. Overall, I found stock camera to work perfectly average. Portrait mode actually worked when I tried it out, showing no signs of excessive blurring. Plenty of detail - as long as you have some lighting on the subject. Darkers areas still suffer and need improvement if it expects to hang with the top tier. 360 CAMERA To get the full experience, I decided to pick up the Essential 360 camera. It’s over priced at retail, but you can find it far cheaper elsewhere. This camera is about a simple as it gets.

Charging: Qualcomm QC 2 is native to all Samsung up to and including S10 Plus. The same 5-9 volt 18 watt charger that Samsung has used for years is included. Both Note9 and S10 Plus also support optional USB C-PD charging. It is not clear if either can support charging 24 watt charging. Using a C-PD charger does not reduce total charging time significantly. When buying a portable battery there is no need to pay more for a power delivery portable battery with a C port. A $20 slim battery with Type A certified QC 3 port works as well and as fast as any. The original cable and compact Samsung wall charger are all that is required.

Excellent, but tricks you need to know to install SIM card.... Phone is excellent. However, there are two tricks to installing the SIM card. First - this phone can take two SIM cards, so there are two slots for the SIM cards. When I first installed the SIM card in the lower slot (closer to the bottom), phone didn't connect to my network/no bars. On line with my provider for 30 min trying to solve problem unsuccessfully. Finally tried moving the SIM card to the other slot. Suddenly the phone worked perfectly. So if you are having a problem connecting to your network, suggest that you try that. Another issue - the phone comes with a transparent flexible case already installed on the phone. Pretty invisible and not at all obvious. Needs to be removed in order to install the SIM card.

Some pros & cons when upgrading from S9 to S20 FE. I took advantage of the T-mobile trade-in program to upgrade my aging early 2018 Samsung S9 64GB to this new late 2020 Samsung S20 FE 128GB which allowed me to get this phone for $200 + taxes. Overall, it's a very good phone for the price even without trade-in, but there are some pros & cons which I'm going to lay out below. *** Pros: - Price / Affordability. Obviously this is the biggest pro of the S20 FE as you can upgrade to one of the newest phones from samsung for not too much without having to shell 1000 dollars or more. - The S20 FE has 6GB of RAM which is an upgrade over the S9's 4GB of RAM.

There isn't much improvement in terms of performance, operability, or battery life over the S9, but at least you know that this S20 FE is close to being the latest and greatest from Samsung for the next couple years until you upgrade again to another iteration... For me, it's a 4/5 star phone and is worth the upgrade from the S9 still but I'm missing my S9 already because it was so good at doing most everything with just one hand... now I got to use 2 hands with this phone most of the time... but at least I have enough onboard fast memory space with 128GB which will allow me to add more apps/take more photos/videos when the apps need the speed of onboard memory to take the photo shot.

The selfie camera also is a big improvement over the S9. - The Fingerprint sensor placement is much better at the front of the handset below the display. A big improvement over the S9 which was at the back of the phone. *** Tie - In terms of overall performance and daily usage, I would say you get about the same performance as the S9. You won't notice that the S20 FE is snappier or slower than the S9 for most apps used. Browsing feels about the same, even though the S20 FE touts the 120Hz display, but has a lower pixel density in terms of screen resolution.

Browsing feels about the same, even though the S20 FE touts the 120Hz display, but has a lower pixel density in terms of screen resolution. Colorwise, they are about the same in terms of vivid colors or contrast/brightness. - In terms of battery life, I see to get about the same performance as my S9, even though the S20 FE touts a larger battery, but also has a bigger display so it evens out. - In terms of 5G performance, I tested it in a few places and I don't see much improvements in terms of Upload or Download performance over 4G LTE. It's very uneven depending on where you are. On T-mobile, I get about 40Mb/s to 90Mb/s downlink with 5G vs 50Mb/s to 75Mb/s with 4G downlink. and around 25Mb/s uplink for 5G and 4G similarly when I'm in a good area.

I am happy with returning my Pixel 2 in a few days. I've been using the Essential Phone for close to a month now, and am currently reviewing it after receiving my Pixel 2 phone a few days ago to test both. After playing around with the controversial camera on both devices, I am happy with returning my Pixel 2 in a few days. Make no mistake, the Pixel 2 has a wonderful camera. Even after sideloading the Google Camera app on to the Essential Phone, there were still noticeable differences in the low-light picture quality and the camera speed. I even compared them both with the iPhone X, and the Pixel 2 still arguably came out on top. But aside from that, I can't say that the Pixel 2 has anything else that I don't get with the Essential Phone, personally.

I got my Essential for $400 (after taking advantage of Amazon's additional $50 gift card promo). And the Pixel 2 is priced at $740 (after the $115 trade-in credit I'd get with my old Nexus). The $300 difference is quite stark at this point. OLED is nice. Sure. But after using the 5.7in display on the Essential, I don't think I can go back to the meager 5in display found in the Pixel 2. The higher contrast attributed to the OLED panel found in the Pixel 2 is nice, but the difference is barely noticeable. The main beneficiary of this technology would be the lower power usage. Which brings me to the battery. The 3000mah battery found in the Essential should make up for the extra juice required to run the LCD panel.

The 3000mah battery found in the Essential should make up for the extra juice required to run the LCD panel. After testing both for the past few days, I can't say if there's a clear winner between the two. The Pixel 2's smaller battery can be compensated by the better software optimization by Google to ensure one full day of use. Essential might still have a few kinks to iron out with their software to ensure they don't unintentionally drain the battery life through poor software optimization. Both have been giving me full-day use with more than enough to spare (25%-50% left in the tank on a good day). In the end, I feel like the Essential is a better match for me. Your opinion and needs might differ, but I hope this review gave you some additional peace of mind before taking the lunge. Cheers!

At first I thought perhaps I just had a buggy individual unit, so I did the troubleshooting steps I'm familiar with such as rebooting, going in and out of airplane mode, etc. Nothing worked. I even completely reset my phone to mfg settings and redid it. Problem still came back. Turns out there are quite a few Moto forum posts about the G7/G7 Power phones having this exact same issue. It is not just my unit - it affects quite a number of them.

It is not just my unit - it affects quite a number of them. The most troubling part was that Moto reps were asking people in these forums to create phone logs and send them in, but this has been going on for months. No updates or fixes and answers no longer being posted in their own forum about it. Not even, "We are working on a fix, thank you for your patience", type of thing. Meanwhile, the problem for many continues. For some tasks it's not a huge deal - you can simply switch off wifi and use LTE to do them. But things like video doorbells and some video security camera apps really do need wifi to work effectively (or, at all) - when you cannot connect to home security apps, yeah, that's a problem.

Excellent value, Good speakers, Good camera. EDIT: The Moto G7 Plus works on AT&T and the companies which use their cell towers, such as Consumer Cellular (including LTE bands) and T-Mobile (possibly not 4G or LTE bands). However, this being an International model, there is no factory warranty in the US. The Moto G7+ takes advantage of major improvements that have been made over recent years in major flagship phones and is able to leverage a good chunk of that technology at a much lower price. At the same time it's not marketed to the people that would necessarily buy a flagship phone, so it still contains certain features that you would more likely find in a mid-range phone, such as a headphone jack. I have using the Moto G7+ for about 2 weeks, and I am impressed with it. Previous to that I used a Sony compact phone since late 2017.

Previous to that I used a Sony compact phone since late 2017. Needless to say, the size of the G7+ took a bit of getting used to, and I find I occasionally miss the ability to do simple things easily with one hand. A few things I’ve noticed: The G7+ has very good speakers (i.e. loud and not tinny or distorted). One is front-facing, and the other, louder one is at the bottom, so in typical use they balance pretty well. The screen is bright enough with good viewing angles. Good WiFi; seems the range is better than other recent phones I've tried. Fine, clear calls and excellent speakerphone function. I’ve only tried the camera a bit but it seems like it works pretty well and is very quick to focus.

I’ve only tried the camera a bit but it seems like it works pretty well and is very quick to focus. In particular, the zoom function is very smooth, and even at high zoom the results are nowhere near as *blocky* as what my previous phones have often produced. The camera interface is simple, with a ring you can move on the screen to specify subject for autofocus/exposure. I've gotten best results leaving HDR on *auto* or always on. I have not had any problems with battery lasting the whole day, but then again I'm someone who most of the time is able to top it up at various different points during the day. As a result it probably never gets below 50% or so.

In general, the G7+ is the first Motorola phone that I have been motivated to try since using the Moto X Pure/Style of 2015, one of my old favorites. The G7+ is much faster, has a better camera, newer software (Android 9 with January 2019 security), and has comparable speakers.

There's no Moto-specific group of apps to rival (or replace) the Google versions of things. Unlike my Sony or ASUS devices, I don't have to deal with a proprietary browser, file manager, photo viewer, contacts app, messenging app, calendar app, clock app, or anything else that's a native part of Android. All the stock Android versions of these things are here, and they all work wonderfully. Also included is the Android Nougat (and Marshmallow) feature that lets you treat an SD card as an extension of internal storage. This feature is REMOVED from Sony, Samsung, and most other devices from major manufacturers. It's present here, so if you want to stick a 128GB SD card into your phone and have it tacked onto the built-in storage, boosting you to over 138GB of internal storage, you can do that.

Tap quickly and you go Home. The extra screen real estate you get from eliminating those soft buttons is nice, and the fingerprint sensor works perfectly. No more trying to type in a PIN, password, or swiping a pattern! The Moto G5 Plus is FAST, too. I'm very happy with how it operates both in the UI and in games. Good and cheap. You’d think only $800+ smartphones are worth it. Then something like the Google Pixel 4a comes along and makes you reconsider. It’s not so much because you’re getting more overall than on a pricier smartphone, but rather it’s the fact that you get a lot for the price of $350 that makes this phone stand out from the pack. The Pixel 4a will tempt even users of high end smartphones to consider the minimalistic, but punchy, approach of Google with this device. It delivers in what matters and it cuts corners where it doesn’t, making us feel uncomfortable about the amounts of money we spend on flagship smartphones. The first thing that will make an impression is the size of the phone. The Pixel 4a is a small phone for 2020. You can handle it with one hand, which says a lot.

The screen is very bright and with nice and accurate colors. The responsiveness of swiping and gestures is great, and I didn’t notice any lag while operating the phone. It’s amazing how good this screen is, especially if you think about the price of this device. On the top left corner you’ll find the punch-hole front camera, used for front facing video and selfies. This is a great move by Google to maximize screen area and minimize the bezels around it. It also contributes in the compactness of the device overall, which could be a decisive factor for many potential buyers. What I love about this device is that is provides a decently large screen (5.8 inches) at a size that can be operated with one hand and is also very lightweight (due to the use of plastics instead of the more premium aluminum or glass).

My index finger keeps going higher and then lower, and also my car mount tends to cover the fingerprint sensor unless I slide the device higher when mounting it. But these are no dealbreakers by any means, especially if you think about the price tag. Things regarding performance are simple. Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 730G isn’t the sharpest processor out there, but Google had no other option for a device priced at $350. Regardless, the 2.2GHz clocked CPU is perfect for average daily use and moderate power consumption. Sure, it won’t impress in gaming, but it will deliver competently in everything else. The 6GB of RAM memory help the Pixel 4a maintain consistency throughout its performance. 4GB have been proven to not be enough for modern smartphones and thankfully Google packed 6GB in the 4a.

4GB have been proven to not be enough for modern smartphones and thankfully Google packed 6GB in the 4a. That, combined with the 128GB of storage space, will allow users to download and install multiple apps without worrying about any shortcomings. Battery autonomy is great too. With 3140 milliamps per hour, and a low powered CPU, you will most probably get more than 1.5 days of operation time before you have to recharge (provided that the average screen time is around a modest 2-2.5 hours/day). The Google Pixel 4a is equipped with a 12 MP rear camera using the IMX363 sensor, with Optical & Electronic Image Stabilization (OIS + EIS). The aperture is f/1.7 and the field of view is 77 degrees. It can shoot 4K videos at 30fps or 1080p video at 60 fps.

It can shoot 4K videos at 30fps or 1080p video at 60 fps. The front facing camera has an 8 MP sensor, an f/2.0 aperture and an 88 degrees field of view. The 4a shoots great pictures with nice colors and good dynamic ranges. The contrast is at a good level as well. Overall the pictures look amazing for a $350 device. I have attached some images that show the same picture shot with the Google Pixel 4a, the iPhone X and the iPhone XR. I am really happy with how the pictures from the 4a turned out. The Pixel 4a of this article is rocking the Android 10, June 2020 build. As all Google Android phones, it has a simple but very smooth and to the point GUI.

As all Google Android phones, it has a simple but very smooth and to the point GUI. Features such as Google Assistant and Call Screening are present in the 4a, as well as advanced AI functionalities that improve several aspects of the phone (for example, AI image processing of the pictures taken by the rear camera). But maybe the most important software “feature” of a Pixel phone is the guaranteed support for at least three years. That means that the Pixel 4a will be receiving Android updates at least until 2023. Overall the Google Pixel 4a is an amazing mid-level smartphone. It offers plenty of features and functionalities at the very reasonable price of $350 dollars. It excels in many areas, and it manages to mask the few deficiencies it has. The 4a is a very affordable way to experience the pure Android world with Google’s great software support.

So far a great experience, beautiful phone. This phone has a ton of love/hate and divided opinions. I have the newer revision white model and it came with stock 7.1.1 Android. Right out of the box I updated it to the last OTA offered, I think I took two total OTA updates with reboots. Being an experienced Nexus phone-haver and rooting/romming/tinkering with 6 different nexus phones and tablets, I also was excited to sideload the 8.0 Oreo beta 2. I unlocked the bootloader and reboot/auto wiped. Then I sideloaded the Oreo beta 2 factory image with no issue.

Then I sideloaded the Oreo beta 2 factory image with no issue. I fully expected to be risking a "beta" experience with this phone due to its reputation, but after all updates and Oreo upgrade, I have not seen any of the issues people slam this phone for. The OS is very smooth, scrolling lag isn't a thing for me, the touch response is slightly less sensitive than my Nexus 6p which I just moved from but isn't a problem. Now the camera app... doesn't take the best quality pictures. Coming into this phone after the devs have been updating the phone and app it isn't as bad as reviews from even a month ago, but compared to the nexus/pixel camera app it still isn't even close. But it does work now.

Phone unlocked by Samsung, not an unlocked phone. They are selling phones that have been unlocked by a code, not that were originally sold unlocked. This means you cannot update the phone unless you use it on a network that it was previously locked to. So, if it was locked to ATT, you cannot update it if you are on Verizon. What this means is that you will never get security/software updates. you cannot remove carrier specific apps, and you don't get features only your carrier offers. Basically, unless you know how to flash the unlocked rom (SM-G970U! XAA variant), you are fkkd. You can find instructions on XDA on how to do this, but it is not a straightforward procedure and certainly not for notices. My phone came with Android 9 and the June security patch, so the software was almost a year old. I'm now on Android 10 with the February patch.

This is a real deal, genuine, 100% functionality Moto G6. 3GB ram, 32 GB internal storage (which you can further increase with an SD card for TRUE integrated storage. I also have its cousin, the Moto G6 Play, which for the version on Virgin has only 2 GB ram and 16 GB storage (although thankfully that's less important here due to Motorola actually integrating your SD card). The G6 Play, however, has an absolutely massive battery capacity (4000 MAh), which this phone sorely lacks. I could get twice as much time without charging compared to this model. The G6 Play also has a Corning Gorilla Glass 3 back. The G6, at least through Tracfone, does not.

The G6, at least through Tracfone, does not. This difference makes the phone feel disappointingly insubstantial and light. The phone has great functionality, handling every app I throw at it with aplomb. Motorola's gesture support is really fun to use, allowing you to screenshot with a "3-finger salute", flick your wrist to activate your camera, or shake your phone like a Maglite to activate the flashlight. Another difference, weirdly enough, is in the charging ports. The G6 Play uses a USB micro connection, whereas the G6 uses the new "standard" (USB-C) that isn't as common as it likely will be in the future. That means your old micro USB plugs will not work. Sound quality is pretty good, although it could be a tad louder. Motorola tends to have a lot of complaints about faulty sound drivers in their phones, but thankfully this one avoided that curse.

I personally desire these features on my smartphone, but manufacturers have been removing them from their flagship smartphones from sometime. I used to only buy smartphone flagships and was always excited to upgrade. I purchased the first Google Pixel XL on launch day back in 2016 and it has been the best phone I’ve ever used. Subsequent Pixel flagships have removed several features I want on my phone or added features I did not want. The Pixel 2 series removed the headphone jack, the Pixel 3XL had an ugly notch mimicking the iPhone X, and the Pixel 4 (non-A) series does not have fingerprint sensors. It really does not make sense that the Pixel 4a, a budget offering, has more features than the Pixel 4, but this is the reality we live in. I’d like to quickly run over the things I love about this device before I start tearing into with criticism. I love that it has a headphone jack.

Even if this phone can get you through morning to night with 10-15% capacity left of a 3,140mah battery, you’ll be left with a battery lasts less long than if you had a 4000mah battery ending the day at 30% before going back on the charger. Lithium-ion cells also degrade as they’re cycled. After 100 cycles a Lithium battery can lose as much as 5%-10% of its capacity. If you start with a larger cell then that degradation will be less of an issue as age sets in. Needless to say, Google fumbled on battery size. I think this is the best new Android phone on the market, but in the same breath, I think that reflects poorly on the Android smartphone market. You might think my criticisms are harsh considering the low price of the phone, but I did not buy this phone because it was cheap.

Best User Experience! Visionary Phone with Amazing Value and Out-of-this-world Build Quality. I was eyeing the Essential phone ever since it was announced. Now, after the price drop, it's almost a no-brainer. If you look at the hardware specifications alone, you don't do this phone justice. Sure, there is no heart-rate monitor, no iris scanner, no wireless charging, not even a headphone jack. It's not an OLED display, there is no optical image stabilization (OIS), no telephoto or wide-angle lens. But there is also no Bixby button, no pre-installed proprietary calendar / app store / file browser bloatware, no screwing around with basic android functionality. Not unlike the Pixel, Nexus, and old Moto phones under Google's control, the Essential PH-1 is about user experience. The Essential PH-1 looks not as sleek as some other flagships, but somehow you want to pick it up and interact with it. Why? It is not annoying.

It is not annoying. Essential gets more stuff right, and - more importantly - less stuff wrong than other companies. Here is what I mean: SOFTWARE EXPERIENCE It's pure Android with basically no modifications (just optimizations). Why is that important? Just three random examples: - Unlike other flagship phones, the Essential PH-1 listens to "OK Google" even if the screen is off and the phone is not connected to a charger. - The Essential PH-1 implements Google's "Cast screen / audio" feature without modifications like strange overlay bubbles. It just works as intended. - When abroad, you see a small R next to you mobile data icon to indicate that you are on roaming. There are no annoying pop-up message every 30 minutes or anything like that. HARDWARE EXPERIENCE Unlike some other flagship phones, this one get's the essentials right.

HARDWARE EXPERIENCE Unlike some other flagship phones, this one get's the essentials right. Like microphones and fingerprint scanner: - The Essential PH-1 uses four microphones for audio input and noise cancellation. Cover whatever part of the phone with your hand / car mount / charging dock and voice commands / hands free calls will still work. - The Essential PH-1 hat an extremely fast, easy to reach fingerprint scanner that works reliably even with swipe gestures turned on. BUILD QUALITY Just wow. This is no fragile all-glass phone. The Essential PH-1 is really slim but feels substantially heavier / rigid than other phones its size: - Unbreakable / unscratchable ceramic back. This is no coated plastic or painted glass. It's colored ceramics which is harder than steal. - Titanium frame (unpainted) with buttons made of the same material. Much stronger than standard aluminum or steel frames.

Much stronger than standard aluminum or steel frames. The plastic antenna lines and the trim (that protects your screen) are colored (not painted) and thus won't loose their color from wear and tear. CAMERA Very basic, but constant software updates by Essential bring more and more functionality. A portrait mode (background blur) was recently introduced and it works very good. The rest of the camera app is very basic with virtually no settings and limited manual controls: - Good user experience (for example there are no integrated half-baked editor and gallery but links from the camera app to the excellent Google Photos app editor and gallery). It lacks features like panorama mode or something like the AI post-processing on Pixel phones, but you can install the Google camera app with full HDR+ compatibility. Unfortunately only the stock camera app can use the monochrome sensor for enhanced low-light shots.

This is really impressive. Essential published the December security update at the very same day as Google did for their Pixel 2 phones. No other company did this. And everything looks extremely promising for future updates - The Essential PH-1 has an open Android 8.0 beta test with detailed instructions for manual installation, covered under warranty. Reports say that the software experience is further improved even in the beta version. - The Essential PH-1 will get hardware abstraction layers (HALs) for much easier and faster updates (Project Treble). While all phones that are released with Android 8 or newer are required to implement Treble, phones updated to Android 8 can choose if they want to support it. Essential is one of only three companies that confirmed Treble support. All the big players will not add support to old phones.

As you assuredly know, if you're reading this review, Essential is a new phone hardware company, and this is their first offering. They've made quite a splash because the company was founded by the guy who invented Android for Google. Darn good bonafides, as they say. The assertion is that this phone, the Essential PH-1, is a smart phone done right. Top end construction, high end components, absolutely no third party bloatware on top of pure Android, and compatible with each and every cell carrier. Oh, let's not forget, overseen by the guy who started the company who, you might expect, as mr. Android, knows how it should be done. Well, promises and anticipation are one thing. Does this phone actually deliver? Before I get to that, let me describe my list of what the "world's best" smart phone SHOULD offer: ░░░░Must haves:░░░░ ❖ Fantastic battery life.

How does the Essential do? ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░ ░░░░Must Haves░░░░: ❖ Battery life: It has good-but-not-great-for-flagship battery life (it made it to the end of the day with normal use, although in my case [I do a lot of surfing during the day], just barely). It's not near as as good as my several year old Droid Turbo and not as good as it could be with the bigger battery in phones made by competitors. The battery is 3040mAh in size. I'll give it half a check mark for this. 0.5 check. ❖ Camera: Oh my. A big disappointment. The Essential uses a dual camera sensor system, one color, one monochrome, and asserts this will allow fabulous pictures even in low light. But... just no. The pictures were all generally very good in good lighting.

The pictures were all generally very good in good lighting. But once the lighting was less than good... they were all over the place--some good, some fuzzy, few outstanding. I compared pictures of the same subjects with a friend who has a Pixel (currently considered by many the best camera phone out there), and it was no contest: In all cases where it wasn't a tie, the Pixel took better shots in the same conditions. The Pixel was also considerably faster in processing pictures. The Essential camera was pretty laggy in taking multiple shots, particularly with HDR on. Reading various information on the Web, there were numerous reports that the camera quality improved with updates so I made sure I had the latest camera update. I did. And the camera wasn't hideous. I mean, this would be considered very good quality relative to phones from a few generations ago.

But a high end phone should provide full control over what's on the phone to advanced users who might want to play with it. ❖ Compatibility with all the major US carriers (Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile, Sprint) and with most world carriers. Because you don't want your expensive phone investment to be a consideration in choosing the best plan. ❖ A good, modern processor: I was ambivalent about even putting this on the list, since each and every modern flagship phone, and even most affordable midline phones, has a processor more than sufficient to provide an entirely acceptable experience. For most users, we are far beyond the point where any negative user experience issues are processor related. But obviously, a slow doggy processor (if you could find one) would be a deal breaker for an ideal phone. ░░░░Should haves:░░░░ ❖ Wireless charging.

I love the matte finish of the Halo Gray model's ceramic back - no fingerprints and super durable. The design is minimal (not even a name or logo to be found) and somewhat industrial, and the extra-tall screen that goes all the way to the top bezel is very useful: it gives you an extra row of icons on your home screen compared to other phones of identical size. Not all apps make use of the extra screen space, but it's better than not having it and very useful when it is used. DISPLAY: The LCD screen looks fantastic. Bright enough for use in direct sunlight, super crisp quad hd resolution, and vivid color reproduction. This screen tends to have a slightly cooler look than some others - not a negative, just a matter of preference. LCD screens may not pop quite like OLED screens, but this one looks great.

Leave it on overnight and the battery will be right where you left it. SOUND: Call quality is very good. No issues hearing others or being heard during calls. The external speaker is average. It's loud enough to get the job done and fine for everyday use, but doesn't distinguish itself from the competition. CAMERA: This is another area where Essential has released numerous updates to improve the phone's performance. Upon it's release, the camera was much maligned for being slow, stripped down, and producing mediocre results. By all accounts the problem was the software rather than the camera hardware. Many users (including me) have installed Google's own camera app and found the phone to be quite capable with a better app. I now find the native app with its many updates to produce results about as good as the Google app.

BIGGEST COMPLAINT: If there is one complaint I have, it's that the touch response of the screen isn't great. It works very well in general use surfing the web, emailing, etc., but in certain games where precise touch recognition is important the phone struggles. This is another issue that seems to have been addressed via software. Before I upgraded the OS to Oreo, swiping to unlock the screen might take 4 or 5 tries. With Oreo, that no longer happens and everything works just fine most of the time. But poor recognition of precise touch movements can be an annoyance in certain games. MAGNETIC ATTACHMENTS: No comment. I like the idea of attaching accessories quickly and easily, but haven't had a chance to test this feature. BOTTOM LINE: Now that Essential has lowered the price of its phone, this is a very attractive offering.

BOTTOM LINE: Now that Essential has lowered the price of its phone, this is a very attractive offering. Moving from my higher priced Galaxy S8+ to the Essential Phone wasn't a big deal at all. About the only thing I really missed was the truly excellent camera performance of the S8+. Pros: fantastic build quality and design (much less fragile than my S8+), excellent performance and power, generous storage, useful larger screen, and beautiful display. Cons: Acceptable but not great camera performance; acceptable but not great external speaker; rare but occasional sub par touch screen response to very precise movements. I would definitely recommend that the Essential Phone be on your short list of midrange priced phones with a lot to offer at a very attractive price.
